Powering Mars: how to provide (more than) enough electrical power to sustain human life on Mars for an extended period of time.

More than enough is a key concept. On Earth we can make plans and construct buildings or cities based on what I like to call 'blue sky' thinking; meaning that everything will be fine as long as the skies are blue and nothing unexpected happens. Ensuring the long term survival of humans on Mars, however, will require us to plan for "rainy days" type of events when everything does not go to plan, when the stuff hits the fan, or when something unexpected or even potentially catastrophic happens.

I like to think of it in the same way that doomsday preparedness types do. One of their maxims is "three is two, two is one, and one is none." So if you have only one of something it might fail or get lost or damaged, then you really have none of that thing. Be it shelter, food, a source of water, etc., one should always expect the unexpected... not entrust your life to a single item or supply of something. But if you have two and one fails, you still have one to use. And having three gives you one to use and one for backup. The same concept should always be applied to living on Mars, in all things.

Calculating the exact power requirements per person is complicated by the fact that everything, from the lights to heat to food and water and even to the very air we breathe, comes at the expense of electrical power. Fortunately it's not rocket science; just maths. The calculations need to be done before any hardware, dare say any human, is sent to Mars... and then add an extra margin for safety sake.

Up till now all the rovers we've sent to Mars have been able to operate on very low power. Solar has been the choice thus far, for the most part. And a problem arose when the solar panels on the rover got covered in dust or at night. But it's only a machine. It can just go into low-power mode and wait. Humans can't do that and neither can the plants we will rely on for food and breathable air. So, although it seems like the easiest and most cost effective way to power a Mars city, solar cannot be the only source of energy, especially when the annual dust storms hit and the entire planet is shrouded by dust cloud. What to do?

One might envision huge banks of batteries able to supply minimal power. But since the dust storm lasts for months at a time that isn't an economical or viable option at all. The same holds true for hydrogen fuel cells. Where does the hydrogen come from? Electrolysis of water is the most likely option. Ok. Where does the water come from? We have to dig it out of the dirt, purify it, and then split it into hydrogen and oxygen -- all of which takes a lot of electrical energy. In either case, we'd need double or triple the amount of solar panels just to provide for night time energy use (forget about months-long dust storms for now) and that would greatly increase launch costs and also increase land use.

So if solar can't be relied upon for life support, then what other options are there? Well, the dreaded ugly N-word: Nuclear. Some of the Mars landers or other space probes have relied on nuclear power of a sort; RTGs, or Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators, which creates electrical energy via radioactive decay of isotopes. RTGs have been used here on Earth in remote locations. The problem is that they only put out a small amount of energy, around 100 watts is the number I hear most often. So it's just not enough power... and I wouldn't recommend sitting one up in your living quarters.

As much as I hate to say it, we need nuclear reactors, not only on Mars but also for any spaceships or other habitations as well.

NASA have come up with a solution, called the kilopower reactor.

Of course, NASA plans to send 4 people to Mars and force them to stay there for 500 days. Studies here on Earth have shown that to be a recipe for disaster as one or more of the crew members is bound to go mental. Humans just don't fare well in isolation or in cramped / antiseptic environments. NASA just doesn't seem to have the ability to learn from their own studies, let alone the numerous studies on isolation done by others. I'd dare to say that any Mars habitat with fewer than 50 or 100 crew members is doomed to failure, one way or another.

I want to see tens of thousands and eventually millions (if not more) humans living on Mars. That would provide a sufficient breeding stock to serve as our "plan B" to ensure the survival of the human species, so that even if an asteroid wiped out the Earth the day after the millionth person landed on Mars we as a species would continue to exist.
